articles.title: Stella McCartney makes waves with ‘sea life, not sea food’ theme in zero-wool Paris show
articles.summary: Designer showcases wool alternatives and ocean-inspired clothes and says ‘kindness requires real work’ Stella McCartney has been talking about animal rights at fashion week for 30 years. She is usually a lone voice, but the issue is back in the headlines this season.
body: “There is no wool on the runway this season, and I’m proud of that,” McCartney said after her show. She has been working on wool alternatives, including Brewed Protein, a fermented alternative to cashmere and wool developed in collaboration with the Japanese biotech firm Spiber, which was first used in her collections a year ago.

The issue, she says, is “a tricky one. I’ve got alpacas at home, and I have to shear them. If you can shear a sheep in a kind, humane way, then I don’t, personally, think that’s the end of the world. When we do have wool in our collections it is responsibly sourced. But the way a lot of [wool production] is done today is deeply cruel.

“At the end of the day it’s about how kind you are, but monitoring that kindness requires real work. At Stella, we police everything from start to finish at my cost, at my time. If I use wool, I can show you exactly where it’s coming from, and I’m proud of that. But I’m alone in that, and I shouldn’t be.”

articles.title: You be the judge: should my girlfriend let me hang my football calendar in her flat?
articles.summary: Kitty is buying a flat and Henry is moving in with her, but they’re already having decor disagreements. You decide who needs to get over their hang-ups? • Find out how to get a disagreement settled or become a juror. It’s not a showroom; it’s a home.
body: My girlfriend Kitty was preparing to buy a flat and I was so proud of her. We were going to move into it together after living in a shared house. I was going to contribute to the mortgage.

The purchase fell through, but our conversations about it highlighted an issue of control. I think I should have some say over what goes into any new home, but when I said I wanted to hang my Liverpool-themed calendar, Kitty put her foot down. She said it was ugly, childish and not her aesthetic.

Kitty works in interiors and has brilliant taste, but this was supposed to be our shared living space. It’s not a showroom; it’s a home. In shared spaces, both people should get a chance to show off their personalities, but also put up with bits that your partner wants. The calendar is a bit of my personality. My mum bought it for me, so it’s not completely trivial, and I love football. It gives me a sense that it’s my home, and I can keep an eye on the dates of the fixtures.
points: Kitty is buying a flat and Henry is moving in with her, but they’re already having decor disagreements.

articles.title: Rachel Roddy’s recipe for lasagne with three cheeses, tomato and tiny meatballs | A kitchen in Rome
articles.summary: A deep and ingredient-busy take on the classic, constructed with four layers of pasta and a little geometric thinking. Bearing in mind that lasagne is a construction, it pays to start with some easygoing geometry.
body: Leave the lasagne to rest for at least 30 minutes, so the flavours can settle and the whole thing firms up, before serving in geometric squares.

Working in a deep frying pan or saucepan on a low heat, warm the olive oil and garlic for a minute or two. Add the fresh and tinned tomatoes and the chilli, stir, then raise the heat so the tomatoes simmer in a lively way for about 20 minutes, mashing them with the back of a spoon to break up any lumps. Once the sauce has lost any wateriness, add salt and a few basil leaves, then set aside.

Squeeze the sausage meat from its casings, then, working with wet hands, form the meat into grape-sized balls. In another frying pan, heat two tablespoons of oil and fry the balls lightly, so they’re almost, but not quite, cooked through.
Beat the ricotta with the milk and some salt to form a soft paste, thinly slice the drained mozzarella and grate the parmesan.
points: A deep and ingredient-busy take on the classic, constructed with four layers of pasta and a little geometric thinking.

articles.title: How AI could ‘supercharge’ election risks across south-east Asia
articles.summary: Some experts fear AI could be weaponised in south-east Asia, home to nations with predominately young and hyper-connected populations. Years ago it would have been an elaborate operation involving an army of cyber troops creating fake news websites, social media accounts and forged dossiers, all…
body: In a worrying sign of how AI could “supercharge” fake news, Anthropic recently revealed how Claude AI was used in a political influence operation in Malaysia. It created a commercial election manipulation platform, utilising a network of about 1,000 X accounts, a fake news outlet called “Malaysia Pulse” and a series of fabricated documents.

The operation appeared designed to target voters in recent state elections, pulling in census and electoral data to exploit sensitive political and social fractures, including race, religion, and royalty across all 222 Malaysian parliamentary constituencies.

The experiment was ultimately ineffective once Anthropic stepped in but has sparked alarm about how AI could be weaponised in future elections in south-east Asia, a region already deeply vulnerable to fake news.
Katie Harbath, who formerly worked on public policy for global elections at Meta, says the case is an example of how AI brings a new level of sophistication and ease to the disinformation landscape.

articles.title: Florence Pugh’s Take on Fall’s Most Divisive Shade Is a Historical Bombshell
articles.summary: “East of Eden” actor Florence Pugh melded the silhouettes of her forthcoming period drama with the season’s most striking shade of chartreuse.
body: Chartreuse is not a color for the faint of heart. Sitting somewhere in the acidic hinterland between yellow and green, it can be tricky enough on a manicure, let alone a red carpet gown. Florence Pugh, however, has never been particularly interested in taking the easy route.

It was bombshell dressing through a distinctly Florence Pugh lens, with a nod to the period drama she’s starring in. Chartreuse is offset with the cooler silver, amped up with the precious metals. Gold, silver, and diamond Bulgari jewelry, including a choker and a smattering of rings, added to the high-shine effect.

Her longtime glam team continued the red carpet rebel’s color story. Makeup artist Alex Babsky painted a smoked-out silver eye beneath sharply defined brows, offset with a soft matte-pink lip. Hairstylist Hyungsun Ju, meanwhile, swept Pugh’s blonde hair into a voluminous layered updo. Even when she’s hitting a more princessy register, it’s still got personality.
points: “East of Eden” actor Florence Pugh melded the silhouettes of her forthcoming period drama with the season’s most striking shade of chartreuse.

articles.title: On the Podcast: Grace Coddington Talks Her New Book and How Fashion Has Changed Since ‘The September Issue’
articles.summary: For this Thursday’s episode of “The Run-Through,” Grace Coddington joined Chloe in the studio for a conversation about her latest book, “Grace: Now,” a massive yellow tome compiling her favorite fashion shoots from the last decade.
body: It was 1968 when Grace Coddington began her career as a fashion editor at British Vogue, going on to cross the pond and spend nearly three decades at Vogue US.

In the opening pages of the book, there is a handwritten tribute to Grace’s late friend Michael Roberts, noting that this was the first major project she had worked on without him in decades. “Michael was someone who could complete my sentences,” Grace tells Chloe. “I’d known him since the early ’70s, so he knew my life very well. He could write and he was a visual person too. I wanted to do it in my handwriting because I felt that I was talking to him. I adored him.”

Later, she reflects on how much has changed since the release of R. J. Cutler’s 2009 documentary The September Issue, in which she was inarguably the breakout star. “Fashion shows were getting bigger and bigger and what you saw was grander and grander. Clothes got much bigger.” Everything seems to have grown except for the magazines, Chloe offers. “I don’t feel it’s about more anymore,” Grace reflects. “It seems obscene to be excessive, with all the things happening in the world.”

articles.title: Connor Storrie and Hudson Williams Are on Opposite Sides of the Fall Knitwear Debate
articles.summary: “Heated Rivalry” stars Connor Storrie and Hudson Williams reunited at the Kate Spade New York Global Summit on Women’s Mental Health sweater weather-ready.
body: If there is one thing Heated Rivalry stars Connor Storrie and Hudson Williams can agree on, it is the merits of a good fall knit. How that knit should look is another matter entirely.

The actors reunited with members of their cast and crew at the Kate Spade New York Global Summit on Women’s Mental Health at The Shed in New York, taking a brief break from filming the second season of their runaway hit series in Canada. And while both arrived dressed for sweater weather, their looks demonstrated the increasingly distinct style identities they have developed since being catapulted into the spotlight.

Storrie, styled by James Yardley, stuck to the polished Saint Laurent uniform that has become his go-to as a house ambassador. He wore a tobacco-brown cashmere sweater layered over a striped cotton-poplin shirt, with slim-cut black wool trousers, a brown leather belt and Bordeaux-red Derbies. It was classic and quite collegiate, in line with Storrie’s most recent turns on the red carpet, made even more sharp by his recently debuted buzzcut.

body: We’re in the midst of a period-drama-packed fall. Before Sense and Sensibility heads to theaters and Pride and Prejudice hits Netflix, another lush literary adaptation is set to dominate the streamer: a new take on John Steinbeck’s magnum opus, the sweeping East of Eden.

Responsible for crafting Cathy-turned-Kate’s knockout, late-19th- and early-20th-century wardrobe was Kirsty Cameron, the New Zealander also behind the intricate costumes in Jane Campion’s The Power of the Dog, another tale of love and loss in the American wilderness. With East of Eden now streaming on Netflix, Cameron talks us through our leading lady’s turbulent, fashion-filled arc—and her own most surprising sources of inspiration.

articles.title: One of Europe's Oldest Cities Is Also an Amazing, Underrated Place to Eat
articles.summary: An Andalusian food scene so often overshadowed by the likes of Seville and Granada is finally stepping out of the shadows.
body: San Sebastián is widely regarded as Spain's culinary capital for good reason: it boasts more Michelin stars per capita than almost anywhere else on earth. But while the pretty, compact Basque seaside city is hard to beat for award-winning pintxos, another part of the country has a gastronomy hub that’s long flown under the radar.

Cádiz, considered western Europe’s oldest continually inhabited city, is often overshadowed by other Andalusian foodie hotspots, like Seville and Granada. It lies in the province of the same name, famed for sought-after bluefin tuna, sharp vinegars and world-class sherry. While celebrated chef Ángel León— the "chef of the sea"—put the province on the global stage when his experimental seafood restaurant Aponiente in nearby Puerto de Santa María became Andalusia’s first establishment to bag three Michelin stars, the wider region’s everyday food culture is just as appetising.

articles.title: Salt Bread (Shio Pan)
articles.summary: Crisp, buttery shell. Soft, flaky center. Cry!
body: Welcome to the Bon Appétit Bake Club, a community of curious bakers. Each month senior Test Kitchen editors Jesse Szewczyk and Shilpa Uskokovic share a must-make recipe and dive deep into why it works. This month we welcome deputy food editor Hana Asbrink to be our guest baker. Come bake and learn with us—and don’t forget to join the Bake Club group chat over on Substack.

The version of this recipe that appeared in our November 2026 print issue has the incorrect bake time listed. The recipe that follows features the correct total bake times of 15-18 minutes (please see step 8).

Salt bread is a wondrous buttery roll known as shio pan in Japanese or sogeum ppang in Korean. It originated in Japan in 2014 and quickly became popularized in Korea soon thereafter, taking off in the post-Covid era around 2021. It's formed by rolling each ball of dough around a nub of salted butter. As it bakes, the butter melts and oozes out of the bun, "frying" and crisping up the bottom. If you can imagine a warm dinner roll meeting a flaky croissant, you're getting closer.
